title: Thyroid, Adrenal & Corticosteroids
summary: Thyroid hormone and antithyroid drugs, glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.

lessons.title: Thyroid Hormone and Replacement

levels.kid: Your thyroid is a little butterfly-shaped gland in your neck. It makes a hormone that works like the gas pedal for your body: it sets how fast you burn energy, how warm you feel, and even how fast your heart beats. To make this hormone, the thyroid needs iodine, which comes from food like iodized salt. If the thyroid is too slow, people feel tired, cold and sluggish. Doctors fix this with a small pill that is a copy of the thyroid's own hormone. It works slowly, so doctors wait a few weeks and then do a blood test to check if the amount is just right.
levels.hs:
The thyroid makes two hormones: **T4** (thyroxine, the main product) and **T3** (the active form). Cells convert T4 into T3. These hormones raise metabolism, heat production and heart rate, and they are essential for brain development in babies.

**Making thyroid hormone:** the gland pulls in iodide from the blood, then an enzyme called **thyroid peroxidase (TPO)** attaches iodine to tyrosines on a big protein called thyroglobulin. These iodinated pieces join to make T4 and T3.

**Control:** the hypothalamus releases TRH, the pituitary releases **TSH**, and TSH tells the thyroid to make hormone. When thyroid hormone is high, it shuts TSH off (negative feedback). So in an underactive thyroid (**hypothyroidism**), TSH rises.

**Treatment:** **levothyroxine** is synthetic T4. It has a long half-life (about a week), so levels stay steady and blood tests are rechecked only after several weeks. It should be taken on an empty stomach, away from calcium, iron and some antacids, which block absorption.

Too much replacement causes hyperthyroid symptoms: fast heart rate, anxiety, bone loss and an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation.
levels.college:
**Synthesis.** Iodide enters follicular cells via the basolateral **sodium-iodide symporter (NIS)**, crosses the apical membrane via pendrin and other channels, and is oxidized and organified onto thyroglobulin tyrosines by **TPO** using H₂O₂ from DUOX enzymes, forming MIT and DIT. TPO also couples DIT + DIT → T4 and MIT + DIT → T3. Thyroglobulin is endocytosed, proteolyzed in lysosomes, and T4 (majority) and some T3 are released; iodide is recycled by dehalogenase (DEHAL1).

**Transport and activation.** More than 99% of circulating T4 and T3 is protein bound (TBG, transthyretin, albumin); only free hormone acts. Cellular uptake uses transporters (MCT8, MCT10, OATPs). **Deiodinases** control local activity: D1 and D2 convert T4 to T3 (D2 is key in brain, pituitary and brown fat), and D3 inactivates T4 to reverse T3 and T3 to T2.

**Action.** T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors (TRα, TRβ), which form heterodimers with RXR on thyroid response elements; unliganded receptors repress, liganded receptors recruit coactivators. Effects: increased Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, thermogenesis, β-adrenergic receptor expression, cardiac myosin and SERCA2 expression (faster contraction and relaxation), and brain myelination.

**Levothyroxine** (T4) is the standard replacement; its long half-life gives stable levels and steady state after about five to six weeks. Absorption is reduced by calcium, iron, PPIs, bile acid sequestrants and celiac disease; enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) increase clearance; estrogen and pregnancy raise TBG and requirements. Start lower in older adults and coronary disease. Monitor TSH (except in central hypothyroidism, where free T4 is used).

**Liothyronine** (T3) has a fast onset and short half-life; it is used in specific situations (some myxedema coma protocols, thyroid cancer withdrawal preparation). **Myxedema coma** is treated with IV levothyroxine (often plus T3) after or with stress-dose hydrocortisone, since coexisting adrenal insufficiency can precipitate crisis.
levels.phd:
**Deiodinase biology.** D2, an ER-resident selenoenzyme, is ubiquitinated and degraded upon T4 binding, a rapid feedback loop that keeps tissue T3 stable when T4 fluctuates. In the pituitary and hypothalamus, D2 generates intracellular T3 that drives TSH suppression; this is why serum T3 alone poorly predicts pituitary feedback. A common D2 polymorphism (Thr92Ala) has been proposed to explain why some patients on levothyroxine report persistent symptoms with normal TSH, prompting trials of combination T4/T3 therapy; results remain inconsistent and guidelines allow cautious trials in selected patients.

**MCT8 and the brain.** MCT8 (SLC16A2) mutations cause Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome: severe neurodevelopmental impairment from cerebral hypothyroidism alongside peripheral thyrotoxicosis with high T3. The T3 analog **tiratricol (Triac)** enters cells independently of MCT8 and improves peripheral thyrotoxicosis; early treatment may help neurodevelopment. This shows that serum hormone levels can mislead when transport is tissue specific.

**Receptor isoform selectivity.** TRβ predominates in liver; TRα in heart and bone. **Resmetirom**, a liver-directed TRβ-selective agonist, reduces hepatic fat and improves fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and was the first approved drug for it, exploiting isoform selectivity to avoid cardiac and bone effects. Resistance to thyroid hormone β (THRB mutations) shows high T4/T3 with non-suppressed TSH; TRα mutations produce a different phenotype with near-normal TSH.

**Non-thyroidal illness.** In critical illness, D1 activity falls and D3 rises (in liver and muscle), lowering T3 and raising reverse T3; TSH may be low. Replacing thyroid hormone in this adaptive state has not improved outcomes, and the pattern reverses with recovery.

**Amiodarone** contains a large iodine load and inhibits D1 and D2 and TR binding, causing hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff persistence) or thyrotoxicosis (type 1 iodine-induced synthesis; type 2 destructive thyroiditis).
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis before treatment.** TSH is the best screen for primary thyroid disease. Do not test during acute illness unless thyroid disease is suspected, because non-thyroidal illness distorts results. Biotin supplements interfere with many immunoassays and can produce false results. In pituitary disease (common in a neurosurgical clinic), TSH can be low or normal despite real hypothyroidism, so measure free T4.

**Starting levothyroxine.** Young healthy adults can start near full replacement; older adults and patients with coronary disease start low and go slow to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmia. Recheck TSH after about six weeks and after any change. Consistency matters more than timing: take it the same way every day, separated from calcium, iron and PPIs. Brand or formulation switches can shift levels. When requirements rise unexpectedly, think of non-adherence, malabsorption (celiac disease, atrophic gastritis), new interacting drugs, weight gain, or pregnancy.

**Pregnancy.** Requirements rise early in pregnancy, so women on levothyroxine should increase their dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, per their physician's plan, and have TSH checked often. Fetal brain development depends on maternal thyroid hormone in the first trimester.

**Subclinical hypothyroidism.** Mild TSH elevation with normal free T4 often does not need treatment, especially in older adults, in whom TSH normally rises.

**Myxedema coma** (hypothermia, altered mental status, hyponatremia, hypoventilation) is an ICU emergency: give stress-dose hydrocortisone first or together, then IV thyroid hormone, with ventilatory support and passive rewarming.

**Neurosurgery angle.** After pituitary surgery, central hypothyroidism may develop over weeks; adrenal function must be assessed and replaced first, because starting thyroid hormone in untreated adrenal insufficiency can trigger adrenal crisis. In hypothyroid patients, anesthesia brings slow drug clearance, hypothermia and hyponatremia, so elective surgery is often delayed until replacement is underway.

keyPoints: NIS imports iodide; TPO organifies and couples iodotyrosines on thyroglobulin to make T4 and T3
T4 is converted to active T3 by deiodinases D1/D2; D3 inactivates (reverse T3)
T3 acts on nuclear TRα/TRβ receptors heterodimerized with RXR
Levothyroxine (T4) has a long half-life; recheck TSH after about six weeks; separate from calcium, iron and PPIs
Use free T4, not TSH, to monitor central hypothyroidism
Myxedema coma: give hydrocortisone before or with IV thyroid hormone

lessons.title: Antithyroid Drugs

levels.kid: Sometimes the thyroid gas pedal gets stuck down, and the body runs too fast. The heart races, the hands shake, people feel hot and can't sit still. This is called an overactive thyroid. Doctors have a few ways to slow it down. Some pills block the thyroid's hormone factory so it makes less. Another pill calms the racing heart and shaky hands while the first pills start working. And sometimes doctors use a special radioactive iodine drink that the thyroid soaks up, which slowly shrinks the overactive part. Doctors pick carefully, especially if someone is pregnant.
levels.hs:
**Hyperthyroidism** means too much thyroid hormone. The most common cause is **Graves' disease**, where antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor. Symptoms: fast heart rate, weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety, and sometimes bulging eyes.

**Treatments:**
- **Thionamides**: **methimazole** and **propylthiouracil (PTU)** block thyroid peroxidase, so the gland makes less hormone. PTU also blocks conversion of T4 to T3 in the body. Methimazole is usually preferred because PTU can cause severe liver damage, but PTU is used in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm.
- **Beta-blockers** like propranolol quickly control the racing heart and tremor but don't fix the thyroid.
- **Radioactive iodine (I-131)**: the thyroid absorbs it and the radiation destroys overactive tissue. Many patients later need thyroid hormone replacement. Not used in pregnancy.
- **Surgery** (thyroidectomy) is another option.

A rare but serious side effect of both thionamides is **agranulocytosis**, a dangerous drop in white blood cells. Patients are told to stop the drug and get a blood count right away if they develop fever or sore throat.

**Thyroid storm** is a life-threatening flare treated in the ICU with several drugs together.
levels.college:
**Thionamides.** Methimazole and PTU are actively concentrated in the thyroid and inhibit **TPO**-catalyzed iodination and coupling. They do not block release of preformed hormone, so stores must deplete over weeks before euthyroidism. PTU additionally inhibits peripheral **type 1 deiodinase**, reducing T4→T3 conversion. Methimazole has a longer intrathyroidal action and fewer serious toxicities; carbimazole is its prodrug.

Adverse effects: rash and arthralgia (common); **agranulocytosis** (rare, usually early, both drugs); **hepatotoxicity**, which is cholestatic with methimazole and hepatocellular, sometimes fulminant, with PTU (boxed warning); ANCA-associated vasculitis with PTU. Teratogenicity: methimazole causes embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal or esophageal atresia) in the first trimester, so PTU is preferred then, with switch to methimazole afterward.

**Radioactive iodine (¹³¹I)** is trapped via NIS and emits β particles destroying follicular cells; effect develops over months. Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; can worsen Graves' orbitopathy (glucocorticoid prophylaxis in at-risk patients, avoid in active moderate-severe disease).

**Iodide** (potassium iodide, Lugol's solution) acutely inhibits hormone release and organification (**Wolff-Chaikoff effect**) and reduces gland vascularity before surgery. In thyroid storm it is given only after a thionamide has been started, so the iodine is not used as substrate for new hormone.

**β-blockers**: propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms and at higher exposure modestly inhibits T4→T3 conversion. **Glucocorticoids** reduce conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency in storm. Bile acid sequestrants reduce enterohepatic recycling. **Perchlorate** competitively blocks NIS (used for amiodarone-induced type 1 thyrotoxicosis). **Lithium** inhibits hormone release.

**Thyroid eye disease**: teprotumumab, an IGF-1 receptor antibody, reduces proptosis; adverse effects include hyperglycemia and hearing impairment.

**Thyroid storm sequence:** β-blocker, then PTU (or methimazole), then iodide after the thionamide, plus hydrocortisone, cooling, fluids and treating the trigger.
levels.phd:
**Mechanism of TPO inhibition.** Thionamides act as preferential substrates for oxidized TPO (compound I), diverting oxidizing equivalents and thereby inhibiting iodination; at higher concentrations they irreversibly inactivate the enzyme. They also may have immunomodulatory effects; TSH receptor antibody levels fall during therapy, and about half of patients with Graves' disease remit after a prolonged course, more likely with small goiters and low antibody titers.

**Agranulocytosis immunology.** Thionamide agranulocytosis has HLA associations (HLA-B*38:02 and HLA-DRB1*08:03 in East Asian populations), suggesting immune-mediated granulocyte destruction; reactive metabolites generated by neutrophil myeloperoxidase may form haptens. Cross-reactivity between methimazole and PTU means switching after agranulocytosis is contraindicated.

**Iodine physiology.** The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is an acute autoregulatory reduction in organification at high intrathyroidal iodide, likely mediated by iodolipids (iodolactones) that inhibit TPO and DUOX. Normal glands escape within days by downregulating NIS; failure to escape (in Hashimoto's thyroiditis, prior radioiodine) causes iodine-induced hypothyroidism. Conversely, the **Jod-Basedow** phenomenon is iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis in autonomous nodules or latent Graves', for example after iodinated contrast.

**Graves' orbitopathy pathogenesis.** Orbital fibroblasts express TSH receptors and IGF-1 receptors that form a signaling complex; stimulation drives hyaluronan production and adipogenesis, expanding orbital tissue. Teprotumumab's success validated IGF-1R crosstalk; small-molecule TSHR antagonists and neonatal Fc receptor blockers (lowering pathogenic IgG) are in development. Smoking strongly worsens orbitopathy and radioiodine response.

**TSH receptor antibodies.** Stimulating antibodies bind the leucine-rich ectodomain and mimic TSH; blocking and neutral antibodies also exist, and shifts between them explain fluctuating thyroid status. Because TSHR antibodies cross the placenta, mothers treated previously with surgery or radioiodine can still have babies with neonatal thyrotoxicosis, a key monitoring point.
levels.expert:
**Choosing treatment for Graves' disease.** Discuss three options: a prolonged course of methimazole (remission in about half), radioactive iodine (definitive, usually causes hypothyroidism), or thyroidectomy (rapid, definitive, used for large goiters, suspicious nodules, severe orbitopathy or pregnancy planning soon). Patient preference matters.

**Before starting a thionamide:** baseline blood count and liver tests. Give written instructions: fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers mean stop the drug and get an urgent white count. Agranulocytosis is treated by stopping the drug, broad-spectrum antibiotics if febrile, and sometimes G-CSF; never rechallenge with either thionamide.

**Pregnancy.** Use PTU in the first trimester, then switch to methimazole; aim for high-normal free T4 using the lowest effective therapy, because thionamides cross the placenta and can cause fetal hypothyroidism and goiter. Check TSH receptor antibodies to predict neonatal disease.

**Thyroid storm** (fever, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, delirium, GI or hepatic dysfunction) is diagnosed clinically; scoring systems help. Treat immediately in ICU: β-blockade (esmolol if unstable or in heart failure, with care), PTU, then iodine after the thionamide, hydrocortisone, cooling and treating triggers like infection, surgery or iodine load. Avoid aspirin for fever because it displaces hormone from binding proteins.

**Iatrogenic triggers.** Iodinated contrast in a patient with toxic nodules can precipitate thyrotoxicosis. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 (destructive) responds to glucocorticoids; type 1 needs thionamides and sometimes perchlorate; mixed forms are common and may require thyroidectomy.

**Neurology angle.** Thyrotoxicosis can present with periodic paralysis (hypokalemic, especially in young Asian men), chorea, tremor, anxiety or atrial fibrillation with cardioembolic stroke. Proximal myopathy is common. Hashimoto's encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy with thyroid antibodies) is a separate, debated entity that enters the differential for unexplained encephalopathy.

Beta-blockers control symptoms; glucocorticoids reduce conversion in storm

lessons.title: Glucocorticoids

levels.kid: On top of your kidneys sit two small glands called adrenal glands. They make a hormone called cortisol, which helps your body handle stress, keeps your blood sugar up, and calms down swelling. Doctors have strong copies of cortisol called steroids, like prednisone. They are like firefighters that put out the fire of inflammation, in things like bad asthma, allergies or swelling around the brain. But these firefighters can also cause trouble if used for a long time: weaker bones, higher sugar, and easier infections. And if someone takes them for a long time, the body's own cortisol factory goes to sleep, so they must be stopped slowly.
levels.hs:
**Glucocorticoids** are steroid hormones. The body's own is **cortisol**, made by the adrenal cortex under control of ACTH from the pituitary. Medicines include hydrocortisone, prednisone, methylprednisolone and dexamethasone.

**How they work:** glucocorticoids enter cells and bind the glucocorticoid receptor. The complex moves into the nucleus and turns genes on or off, which is why their effects take hours to develop.

**What they do:**
- Strongly reduce inflammation and suppress the immune system (used for asthma, allergies, autoimmune disease, transplant rejection)
- Raise blood glucose
- Break down muscle and bone over time
- Redistribute fat to the face and abdomen

**Neuro uses:** **dexamethasone** dramatically reduces brain swelling around tumors, and it is given in some types of bacterial meningitis.

**Side effects with long-term use:** weight gain, high blood sugar, osteoporosis, cataracts, infections, mood changes, poor wound healing, and slowed growth in children.

**The big safety rule:** long-term steroids suppress the body's own cortisol production. Stopping suddenly can cause **adrenal crisis**, so doses are tapered slowly. Inhaled and topical steroids reduce whole-body side effects.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Glucocorticoids diffuse into cells and bind the cytosolic **glucocorticoid receptor (GR)**, releasing HSP90 chaperones; the complex dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus. **Transactivation**: GR dimers bind glucocorticoid response elements, inducing anti-inflammatory genes (annexin A1/lipocortin, which inhibits phospholipase A2; MKP-1; GILZ; IκBα) and metabolic genes (PEPCK, glucose-6-phosphatase, tyrosine aminotransferase). **Transrepression**: GR monomers tether to and inhibit NF-κB and AP-1, reducing cytokines, COX-2, adhesion molecules and iNOS. Many metabolic adverse effects track transactivation, and many anti-inflammatory effects track transrepression. Rapid non-genomic effects occur at high exposure.

**Cellular effects.** Lymphopenia (redistribution and apoptosis), eosinopenia, monocytopenia; **neutrophilia** from demargination and marrow release; reduced antigen presentation and T-cell activation.

**Agents.** Relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity guide use: hydrocortisone (equal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid action; replacement and stress therapy), prednisone (prodrug activated by hepatic 11β-HSD1 to prednisolone), methylprednisolone (pulses), **dexamethasone** and betamethasone (long-acting, about 25–30 times hydrocortisone's anti-inflammatory potency, essentially no mineralocorticoid activity; used for cerebral edema and fetal lung maturation). Budesonide has high first-pass metabolism (gut-targeted Crohn's therapy, inhaled use).

**Adverse effects.** Iatrogenic Cushing's (central obesity, striae, moon face), hyperglycemia, osteoporosis (osteoblast inhibition; prevention with calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates), avascular necrosis of the femoral head, myopathy (proximal; critical illness myopathy with neuromuscular blockers), cataracts and glaucoma, peptic ulcer risk mainly with NSAIDs, psychiatric effects (insomnia, mania, psychosis), infection risk including *Pneumocystis*, growth suppression, and **HPA axis suppression**.

**Neurosurgical uses.** Dexamethasone reduces **vasogenic** edema around tumors and abscesses by tightening the blood-brain barrier; it does not help **cytotoxic** edema from stroke. In traumatic brain injury, the CRASH trial showed corticosteroids **increased** mortality, so they are contraindicated. In acute spinal cord injury, high-intensity methylprednisolone is no longer standard. Dexamethasone before antibiotics reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.
levels.phd:
**GR structural biology.** The GR's ligand-binding domain positions helix 12 to create an AF-2 coactivator groove; agonist potency reflects both affinity and coactivator recruitment efficiency, so 'potency' is tissue and gene specific. Fluorination at C9 (dexamethasone) and a 1,2 double bond (prednisolone) increase glucocorticoid potency and reduce mineralocorticoid activity; a 16-methyl blocks MR binding. GR binding sites are largely determined by pre-existing chromatin accessibility set by pioneer factors like AP-1 and FOXA, which explains cell-type-specific responses.

**Revisiting the transactivation/transrepression model.** The simple 'dimer = side effects, monomer = benefits' model is incomplete: some anti-inflammatory effects need transactivation (GILZ, DUSP1/MKP-1, TTP destabilizing cytokine mRNA), and GR dimerization-defective mice still develop some side effects. Even so, **dissociated** agonists like vamorolone (a Δ9,11 steroid that lacks key transactivation contacts and acts as an MR antagonist) were approved for Duchenne muscular dystrophy with less growth and bone impact than prednisone, a partial validation.

**Pre-receptor metabolism.** 11β-HSD1 (liver, adipose, bone, brain) regenerates cortisol from cortisone and activates prednisone; 11β-HSD2 (kidney, colon, placenta) inactivates cortisol, protecting MR and the fetus. Prednisolone is partly inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2, whereas dexamethasone and betamethasone cross efficiently, which is exploited for fetal lung maturation and avoided when maternal-only treatment is intended.

**Steroid resistance.** Mechanisms include GRβ isoform expression (a dominant-negative splice variant), reduced HDAC2 activity from oxidative stress (smoking, COPD), MAPK phosphorylation of GR, and increased P-glycoprotein efflux.

**Brain edema physiology.** Dexamethasone upregulates tight junction proteins (occludin, claudin-5) and angiopoietin-1 while downregulating VEGF, restoring barrier function around tumors within hours to days. It also has oncologic consequences: in glioblastoma, corticosteroid use correlates with worse survival in some analyses and blunts immunotherapy, driving interest in steroid-sparing options like bevacizumab for edema.
levels.expert:
**Prescribing well.** Use the lowest effective exposure for the shortest time, prefer local delivery (inhaled, topical, intra-articular) and plan the exit before starting. For anticipated courses longer than a few weeks: bone protection (calcium, vitamin D, consider bisphosphonate), *Pneumocystis* prophylaxis when combined immunosuppression or prolonged high-intensity therapy is present, glucose monitoring, eye checks with long-term use, gastroprotection when combined with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, and screening for latent TB, hepatitis B and Strongyloides in people from endemic areas before major immunosuppression (Strongyloides hyperinfection can be fatal).

**Neurosurgical practice.** Dexamethasone is the standard for symptomatic peritumoral vasogenic edema and spinal cord compression from metastases; taper as soon as the mass is treated. Avoid empiric steroids when primary CNS lymphoma is possible until biopsy, because steroids can shrink lymphoma and make the biopsy non-diagnostic. Do not use steroids in traumatic brain injury. Watch for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, delirium and wound complications after craniotomy, and remember that steroid myopathy can masquerade as new weakness.

**Meningitis.** In suspected bacterial meningitis in adults in high-income settings, give dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose; continue if pneumococcus is confirmed.

**HPA axis.** Anyone on prolonged systemic glucocorticoids (generally beyond about three weeks, or with Cushingoid features) should be assumed suppressed: they need tapering and stress coverage during surgery or serious illness. Inhaled fluticasone combined with a strong CYP3A inhibitor (ritonavir, cobicistat, itraconazole) can cause Cushing syndrome and then adrenal crisis when stopped.

**Psychiatric effects** are dose related; ask about sleep and mood, and involve psychiatry early for mania or psychosis rather than stopping abruptly.

lessons.title: Mineralocorticoids and Adrenal Insufficiency

levels.kid: Your adrenal glands make another hormone called aldosterone. It is the body's salt-and-water manager. It tells the kidneys, 'Keep the salt, and water will stay too,' which keeps blood pressure steady. If the adrenal glands stop working, there isn't enough cortisol or aldosterone. People feel very tired and dizzy, and in a big emergency their blood pressure can crash. Doctors give replacement pills to copy the missing hormones. People who need them carry an emergency shot and wear a medical bracelet, and when they get sick, they take extra medicine, like giving the body a little more help on a hard day.
levels.hs:
**Aldosterone** is the main **mineralocorticoid**. Made in the outer layer of the adrenal cortex, it is released in response to angiotensin II (from the renin system) and high potassium. It acts on the kidney's collecting duct to retain sodium (and water) and excrete potassium and acid.

**Drugs:**
- **Fludrocortisone** is a synthetic mineralocorticoid used to replace aldosterone.
- **Spironolactone** and **eplerenone** block aldosterone's receptor. They raise potassium and are used for heart failure, resistant hypertension and excess aldosterone. Spironolactone can cause breast enlargement in males because it also blocks androgen receptors.

**Adrenal insufficiency** means not enough cortisol:
- **Primary** (Addison's disease): the adrenal glands are damaged, often autoimmune. Both cortisol and aldosterone are low. ACTH is high, which darkens the skin.
- **Secondary**: the pituitary doesn't make enough ACTH. Aldosterone is usually fine, because it's controlled by the renin system.
- **Most common cause overall**: stopping long-term steroid medicines, which had put the body's own system to sleep.

**Adrenal crisis** (shock, vomiting, confusion, low sodium, high potassium) is an emergency: give IV **hydrocortisone** and fluids immediately, without waiting for test results.
levels.college:
**Aldosterone physiology.** The zona glomerulosa expresses aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2); angiotensin II (AT1, Gq) and hyperkalemia (depolarization opening Ca²⁺ channels) stimulate secretion, ACTH acutely. Aldosterone binds the **mineralocorticoid receptor (MR)** in principal cells, inducing **SGK1** (which prevents Nedd4-2-mediated ENaC removal), ENaC, ROMK and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, increasing Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ and H⁺ secretion. MR binds cortisol with equal affinity; **11β-HSD2** converts cortisol to cortisone in aldosterone-target cells, conferring specificity. Inhibition by glycyrrhetinic acid (licorice) or saturation by massive cortisol (ectopic ACTH) causes apparent mineralocorticoid excess: hypertension, hypokalemia, alkalosis.

**MR antagonists.** Spironolactone (steroidal, nonselective: antiandrogenic, progestogenic effects; gynecomastia, menstrual changes; active metabolites such as canrenone), eplerenone (more selective, CYP3A4 metabolized), and **finerenone** (nonsteroidal, balanced tissue distribution; reduces kidney and cardiovascular events in diabetic CKD). All cause hyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors/ARBs and CKD. Benefits in heart failure (RALES, EMPHASIS-HF) exceed blood pressure effects, reflecting anti-fibrotic actions.

**Fludrocortisone** (9α-fluorinated hydrocortisone) has strong MR activity; used in primary adrenal insufficiency and sometimes orthostatic hypotension and cerebral salt wasting. Adverse: hypertension, edema, hypokalemia.

**Adrenal insufficiency.** Primary (autoimmune adrenalitis, TB, hemorrhage in sepsis or anticoagulation, metastases, congenital adrenal hyperplasia): low cortisol and aldosterone, high ACTH and renin, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia. Secondary/tertiary (pituitary or hypothalamic disease, exogenous glucocorticoids, opioids, checkpoint inhibitor hypophysitis): low ACTH, intact aldosterone, hyponatremia from cortisol deficiency (impaired free-water excretion) but no hyperkalemia. Diagnosis: early-morning cortisol and ACTH, then **cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test**.

**Replacement.** Hydrocortisone in divided doses mimicking the diurnal rhythm (or prednisolone), plus fludrocortisone in primary disease. **Crisis:** IV hydrocortisone at high exposure (which also provides mineralocorticoid action), saline with dextrose; draw cortisol/ACTH first if it causes no delay. If testing must follow, dexamethasone does not interfere with cortisol assays.

**Drugs causing adrenal insufficiency:** etomidate (11β-hydroxylase inhibition), ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, mitotane, and abrupt withdrawal of glucocorticoids.
levels.phd:
**MR in the brain and heart.** In hippocampus and many non-epithelial tissues, 11β-HSD2 is absent and MR is occupied mostly by cortisol, acting as a high-affinity glucocorticoid receptor regulating stress responses, while lower-affinity GR handles stress peaks. In cardiomyocytes and vasculature, MR activation under oxidative stress or high salt drives inflammation, fibrosis and endothelial dysfunction, which explains antagonist benefits even when aldosterone is normal. Nonsteroidal MR antagonists like finerenone are bulky ligands that inhibit coactivator recruitment and have more even heart/kidney distribution than spironolactone, which concentrates in kidney, possibly lowering hyperkalemia risk per unit of benefit.

**Aldosterone breakthrough and synthase inhibitors.** Chronic ACE inhibition is followed by rising aldosterone in many patients. Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) inhibitors like baxdrostat and lorundrostat lower blood pressure in resistant hypertension; selectivity over CYP11B1 (93% identical, cortisol synthesis) was the medicinal chemistry challenge, since cross-inhibition causes adrenal insufficiency.

**Congenital adrenal hyperplasia** (21-hydroxylase deficiency) diverts precursors to androgens; salt-wasting crises occur in infancy. CRF1 receptor antagonists (crinecerfont) lower ACTH-driven androgen excess and allow lower glucocorticoid exposure, a new strategy.

**Glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency.** Recovery of CRH and POMC neurons and of adrenal fasciculata can take months. Morning cortisol thresholds stratify likelihood of recovery, but responses to stress, not basal secretion, are what matter clinically. Variability is large: some patients on modest inhaled or intra-articular steroids are suppressed, especially with CYP3A inhibitors.

**Vasopressin, cortisol and sodium.** Cortisol deficiency removes tonic inhibition of CRH and vasopressin co-secretion in parvocellular neurons, raising ADH and causing dilutional hyponatremia indistinguishable from SIADH. Excluding adrenal insufficiency (and hypothyroidism) is therefore part of every SIADH diagnosis, especially after pituitary surgery or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
levels.expert:
**Spot the crisis.** Unexplained hypotension unresponsive to fluids and pressors, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypoglycemia, especially in someone on long-term steroids, after pituitary surgery, with known autoimmune disease, on checkpoint inhibitors, or with a fall and anticoagulation (adrenal hemorrhage), should trigger immediate IV hydrocortisone. Draw a random cortisol and ACTH if possible, but never delay treatment. Treat precipitants like infection.

**Patient education saves lives.** Sick-day rules: temporarily increase glucocorticoid intake during fever or significant illness according to the written plan; use the emergency injectable hydrocortisone if vomiting prevents oral intake, then seek care. Wear medical identification and carry a steroid emergency card. Schedule surgery with stress coverage, adjusted to surgical severity.

**Neurosurgical and ICU pearls.** Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery: patients with preoperative adrenal insufficiency receive perioperative hydrocortisone; others often have postoperative morning cortisol checks, with replacement when low. After Cushing's disease resection, low cortisol signals cure, and patients need replacement for months while the suppressed axis recovers. In subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral salt wasting is sometimes treated with fludrocortisone or hypertonic saline, while fluid restriction is avoided because hypovolemia worsens vasospasm risk. Etomidate for intubation causes transient adrenal suppression; its significance in sepsis remains debated.

**Septic shock.** Hydrocortisone is added for shock requiring escalating vasopressors; it speeds shock reversal, though mortality effects differ across trials. This is different from treating true adrenal insufficiency.

**Hyperkalemia vigilance.** MR antagonists with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements or CKD need potassium checks soon after starting and regularly; this combination produced a surge of hyperkalemia admissions after RALES.

**Primary hyperaldosteronism** is common in resistant hypertension and hypokalemia; screen with an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, because unilateral adenomas are surgically curable.

keyPoints: Aldosterone acts on MR in principal cells (via SGK1, ENaC, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to retain Na⁺ and excrete K⁺ and H⁺
11β-HSD2 protects MR from cortisol; its inhibition (licorice) causes apparent mineralocorticoid excess
Spironolactone (antiandrogenic), eplerenone and finerenone block MR; all cause hyperkalemia
Primary adrenal insufficiency: low cortisol and aldosterone, high ACTH, hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia; secondary preserves aldosterone
The most common cause of adrenal insufficiency is withdrawal of exogenous glucocorticoids
Adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone and fluids immediately; do not delay for tests

lessons.title: Pituitary and Hypothalamic Drugs

levels.kid: Deep in your head, under your brain, is a tiny gland the size of a pea called the pituitary. It is the boss of many other glands, sending out messages that say 'grow,' 'make thyroid hormone,' or 'save water.' Right above it, the hypothalamus is the boss's boss. Doctors have medicines that copy these messages or block them. Growth hormone helps kids who are not growing because they lack it. A medicine called desmopressin acts like the body's 'save water' message for people who pee too much. And some pills can shrink certain pituitary lumps without surgery. Brain surgeons work closely with these medicines.
levels.hs:
The **hypothalamus** releases hormones that control the **pituitary**, which then controls the thyroid, adrenals, gonads, growth and water balance. Doctors use drugs that copy or block these signals.

**Anterior pituitary drugs:**
- **Growth hormone (somatropin)** treats children and adults with true GH deficiency.
- In **acromegaly** (too much GH, usually from a pituitary tumor), doctors use **somatostatin analogs** (octreotide, lanreotide) that turn GH down, and **pegvisomant**, which blocks the GH receptor.
- **Prolactinomas** (prolactin-making tumors) are treated first with pills called **dopamine agonists** (cabergoline, bromocriptine), because dopamine naturally turns prolactin off. They often shrink the tumor, even large ones, so surgery may not be needed.

**Posterior pituitary drugs:**
- **Vasopressin** (ADH) helps the kidneys save water and also squeezes blood vessels.
- **Desmopressin** (DDAVP) is a version that mainly saves water. It treats **diabetes insipidus**, where people make huge amounts of dilute urine, common after pituitary surgery.
- **Vaptans** (tolvaptan) block ADH and treat low sodium from too much ADH (SIADH).
- **Oxytocin** causes uterine contractions in labor and helps control bleeding after birth.

The main danger with water hormones is sodium that is too low or changes too quickly.
levels.college:
**Growth hormone axis.** GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits GH release; GH acts via JAK2/STAT5 to produce hepatic **IGF-1**. Recombinant **somatropin** treats GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome and others; long-acting analogs now exist. Adverse: edema, arthralgia, insulin resistance, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis. **Mecasermin** (recombinant IGF-1) treats primary IGF-1 deficiency (GH receptor defects); hypoglycemia is the key risk.

**Acromegaly.** **Somatostatin analogs** (octreotide, lanreotide; SSTR2-preferring; pasireotide binds SSTR5 more and causes marked hyperglycemia) lower GH and IGF-1 and can shrink tumors; adverse: gallstones, GI effects, bradycardia. **Pegvisomant** is a modified GH that binds the receptor but prevents functional dimerization; monitor **IGF-1** (GH rises), and liver tests. Cabergoline helps mildly elevated IGF-1. Surgery is first line for most.

**Prolactin.** Dopamine via D2 receptors tonically inhibits lactotrophs. **Cabergoline** (long-acting, better tolerated, preferred) and bromocriptine normalize prolactin and shrink most prolactinomas, even macroadenomas with visual compromise. Adverse: nausea, orthostatic hypotension, impulse control disorders, and valvulopathy (5-HT2B agonism) at the high exposures used historically in Parkinson's.

**Cushing's disease** drugs: pasireotide, osilodrostat and metyrapone (11β-hydroxylase inhibitors), ketoconazole/levoketoconazole, and mifepristone (GR antagonist).

**Posterior pituitary.** Vasopressin acts on V1a (vasoconstriction; used in vasodilatory shock and variceal bleeding), V1b (ACTH release) and V2 receptors (collecting duct, Gs → cAMP → aquaporin-2 insertion; also von Willebrand factor and factor VIII release). **Desmopressin** is V2-selective with negligible pressor effect; uses: central diabetes insipidus, hemophilia A/von Willebrand disease type 1, nocturnal enuresis. Risk: **hyponatremia** and seizures from water retention. **Vaptans**: tolvaptan (oral V2 antagonist; hyponatremia, ADPKD; hepatotoxicity) and conivaptan (IV V1a/V2). Correct chronic hyponatremia slowly to avoid **osmotic demyelination**.

**Oxytocin** induces labor and treats postpartum hemorrhage; excess causes uterine hyperstimulation and water intoxication (it has V2-like antidiuretic action).
levels.phd:
**GH receptor pharmacology.** GH binds a preformed GHR dimer via two asymmetric sites; site 1 is high affinity, site 2 triggers rotation of the receptor transmembrane helices that activates JAK2. Pegvisomant carries site 1 enhancing mutations and a G120R substitution that abolishes site 2 binding, making it a receptor-occupying antagonist; pegylation extends half-life but reduces affinity, compensated by the site 1 mutations. Because it does not act on the tumor, tumor growth must be watched with MRI.

**Somatostatin receptor subtypes.** Five SSTRs (Gi-coupled) differ in distribution: somatotroph adenomas mostly express SSTR2, corticotroph adenomas SSTR5 (hence pasireotide for Cushing's disease). Pasireotide's hyperglycemia arises from SSTR5-mediated suppression of insulin and incretin secretion with relative sparing of glucagon. Radiolabeled somatostatin analogs are used for imaging and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy of neuroendocrine tumors.

**Dopamine agonist resistance and mechanism.** Cabergoline acts via D2 short and long isoforms, inhibiting adenylate cyclase and prolactin gene transcription and causing lactotroph shrinkage; resistance correlates with reduced D2 expression. Withdrawal after years of normoprolactinemia succeeds in a minority, more often when no residual tumor is visible. Rapid tumor shrinkage can cause CSF rhinorrhea when the adenoma had invaded the sellar floor, a neurosurgical complication of medical therapy.

**Water balance after pituitary surgery.** Injury to the stalk or posterior lobe produces a **triphasic response**: early diabetes insipidus (axonal shock), then a SIADH-like phase from unregulated release of stored vasopressin from degenerating terminals, then permanent DI if enough magnocellular neurons die. Isolated delayed hyponatremia around a week after surgery is a frequent cause of readmission. Desmopressin given in the second phase can cause profound hyponatremia, so treatment is guided by serial sodium and urine output.

**V2 receptor genetics.** X-linked nephrogenic DI arises from AVPR2 loss of function; gain of function causes nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, which, unlike SIADH, does not respond to vaptans. Pharmacological chaperones (cell-permeable V2 antagonists) can rescue misfolded AVPR2 trafficking, an example of chaperone therapy for GPCR misfolding.
levels.expert:
**The pituitary patient.** Before and after any pituitary surgery, assess every axis: cortisol first (replace before thyroid hormone), then thyroid, gonadal, GH and water balance. Visual fields and MRI anchor decisions.

**Prolactinoma is a medical disease first.** Even a macroprolactinoma compressing the optic chiasm is usually treated with cabergoline, with visual improvement often within days to weeks; surgery is for intolerance, resistance, apoplexy or CSF leak. Beware the **hook effect**: a giant prolactinoma can show falsely modest prolactin if the sample is not diluted, which might lead to misdiagnosis as a non-functioning adenoma and unnecessary surgery. Also distinguish true prolactinomas from stalk effect, where any sellar mass modestly raises prolactin by blocking dopamine delivery. Screen for impulse control problems on dopamine agonists. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide (D2 blockers) cause hyperprolactinemia.

**Post-transsphenoidal surgery water balance.** Track urine output, urine specific gravity or osmolality and serum sodium closely. Diagnose DI with large volumes of dilute urine plus rising sodium, not urine volume alone, and avoid reflexive desmopressin in patients who can drink to thirst. Watch for delayed hyponatremia around the end of the first week; many centers give fluid-restriction advice at discharge.

**Hyponatremia rules.** Find the cause (volume status, urine osmolality and sodium, cortisol and thyroid). In severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma), give hypertonic saline boluses to stop symptoms, then limit correction to avoid osmotic demyelination, using desmopressin 'clamp' strategies when overcorrection threatens. Do not use vaptans with hypertonic saline or in hypovolemic patients, and avoid tolvaptan in liver disease.

**Apoplexy** (sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia from hemorrhage into an adenoma) needs immediate hydrocortisone and urgent neurosurgical evaluation.

**Vasopressin in neurocritical care** is a useful vasopressor in septic shock, but it lowers urine output and can drop sodium; monitor closely in brain-injured patients where hyponatremia worsens edema.

keyPoints: Somatropin replaces GH; mecasermin replaces IGF-1 in GH-receptor defects
Acromegaly: somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide; pasireotide causes hyperglycemia) and pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist; monitor IGF-1)
Prolactinomas are treated first with dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred), even macroadenomas
Desmopressin is V2-selective for central DI, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease; risk is hyponatremia
Vaptans block V2 for SIADH; correct chronic hyponatremia slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
After pituitary surgery: watch for the triphasic response (DI, SIADH, permanent DI)
